title: Tracing Typos in LLMs: My Attempt at Understanding How Models Correct Misspellings
primary_claim: A single attention head (L0H3) in Llama-3.2-1B, a 'subword merging head' that moves information between subword tokens of the same word, is the primary component responsible for typo correction when no surrounding context is available; ablating it breaks typo correction (measured via logit difference) while leaving normal text and general MLP-driven performance unaffected.
quote: With this setup, only the subword merging head (L0H3) shows a significant impact. That suggests, that the previous plot with loss was a bit misleading and that the loss was probably influenced by other factors.
metric: logit difference change upon single-head ablation
target_value: only the subword merging head (L0H3) showed a significant impact on logit difference when ablated one-by-one across all attention heads
tolerance_rationale: other scalar metric: 15% relative; post reported no spread, tolerance is a guess

needed: hand-written sentence lists embedded directly in the notebook

blockers: No requirements.txt/environment file -- dependency versions are entirely unpinned (%pip install with no version numbers); the notebook appears Colab-authored (login("Your hf token") placeholder, inline package installs).
inspector_notes: Single unpolished exploratory notebook (README calls it 'rough, unpolished'), 104 cells, no separate scripts. Cheap to rerun; main risk is environment drift from unpinned transformer_lens/circuitsvis versions, not compute. No closed-API usage found.
headline_artifact: Notebook cells computing logit-difference before/after ablating each attention head one-by-one, identifying L0H3 as the only head with significant impact
